object_types.name: Account
object_types.definition: A customer account; everything (subscriptions, billing) hangs off this.

source_references.excerpt: An account. Every account has an account number. That's what everything hangs off.
Yes. Six digits, sequential, never reused.

object_types.name: Subscription
object_types.definition: The agreement that an account pays a given amount on a given cycle for a given product/plan.

source_references.excerpt: A subscription is the agreement that this account pays us this amount on this cycle for this thing. It's got a subscription ID.
Unique. Generated, prefixed with SUB.

object_types.name: Product
object_types.definition: A product sold by the company, e.g. CORE, ANALYTICS, CONNECT.

source_references.excerpt: Product code. We have three: CORE, ANALYTICS, and CONNECT.

object_types.name: Price Plan
object_types.definition: The billing artefact that says what the customer pays and how often; generates the invoice line.

source_references.excerpt: The price plan. It's got a plan code, it says what the customer pays and how often. CORE-MO-49, CORE-AN-490, that kind of thing.
And I mean the billing artefact. The thing that generates the invoice line.

object_types.name: Feature Bundle
object_types.definition: The feature/entitlement bundle a customer gets (seats, API access, SSO); the thing on the pricing page.

source_references.excerpt: When I say plan I mean what the customer gets. Starter, Professional, Enterprise. It's the feature bundle -- how many seats, whether they get the API, whether they get SSO.
Name. Starter, Professional, Enterprise. There's no code, which annoys me. ... Yes. There's exactly one Professional.

object_types.name: Plan Change
object_types.definition: A record of a change to a subscription's price plan, with effective date and requester.

source_references.excerpt: A change is a record. We don't overwrite the plan on the subscription, we write a plan change with an effective date... It's got a change ID.

object_types.name: Start Date
object_types.definition: The date a subscription begins; always present.

source_references.excerpt: Start date is always there. You can't create a subscription without one, the form won't submit.

object_types.name: End Date
object_types.definition: The date a subscription ends; optional, present for fixed-term subscriptions or set on cancellation of annual subs.

source_references.excerpt: An open-ended subscription has no end date. Most of them are open-ended -- they run until cancelled. A fixed-term one has an end date agreed up front

object_types.name: Billing Period
object_types.definition: The billing cycle of a subscription.

source_references.excerpt: Monthly or annual.
Only those two. There was a quarterly once, for one customer, and it caused so much trouble that we bought them out of it.

object_types.name: Subscription Status
object_types.definition: The status of a subscription for finance reporting purposes.

source_references.excerpt: Trialing, active, past due, cancelled.

object_types.name: Paused Flag
object_types.definition: A separate boolean flag indicating a subscription is paused; not part of the status enumeration, overlaps confusingly with active status.

source_references.excerpt: Paused isn't a status, it's a flag. ... It behaves like a status but it isn't one, it's a separate boolean, which is exactly why it causes bugs.

object_types.name: Effective Date
object_types.definition: The date a plan change takes effect.

source_references.excerpt: It has to, because we need to know who made it and when it takes effect, and those are different dates.

object_types.name: Change Made Date
object_types.definition: The date a plan change was made/requested (as distinct from effective date).

source_references.excerpt: Someone can make a change on the third that takes effect on the first of next month.

object_types.name: Requester
object_types.definition: The person who requested a plan change.

source_references.excerpt: It records the subscription, the new price plan, the effective date, and who requested it.

object_types.name: MRR
object_types.definition: Monthly recurring revenue; a derived number normalising plan price to a month, not stored.

source_references.excerpt: Every subscription has an MRR. Monthly recurring revenue. It's the number I live in.
It's worked out. It's the plan price normalised to a month. An annual plan at 490 is an MRR of 40.83.

ambiguities.description: The term 'plan' is used for at least three different concepts: Priya's 'price plan' (billing artefact, plan code), Tom's 'feature bundle' (what customer gets, e.g. Starter/Professional/Enterprise), and a third informal 'plan' used by the sales team referring to a negotiated deal that frequently matches neither. Only the first two are modeled; the sales-team 'deal' concept is explicitly deferred to another meeting and not captured.

source_references.excerpt: So we've got two things both called plan. ... We've got two things both called plan, and the sales team calls a third thing a plan, which is the deal they negotiated, which frequently matches neither. ... Don't. That's a different meeting.

ambiguities.description: Whether Account and 'Customer' (company) are the same identity is unclear: if an account closes and the same company returns, they get a new account number and are treated as a new customer for reporting purposes, even though Tom considers it the same company from a product perspective. This suggests Account and 'real-world Customer/Company' may be distinct concepts, but only Account is modeled per the stated rule.

source_references.excerpt: If an account closes and the same company comes back, they get a new number and we treat them as a new customer for reporting. ... Which drives me mad, incidentally, because from a product perspective it's the same company and we lose the history.

ambiguities.description: The 'one active subscription per account per product' rule's exact scope is unclear -- it was originally stated as 'one active subscription' (period), then revised to 'one active subscription per product' after clarification that there are now three products. It's unclear if there are other exceptions or if this could change again with the fourth product in discovery.

source_references.excerpt: How many subscriptions can an account have? ... One. ... One active one. ... ...Let me be careful, because I nearly told you something wrong. An account has one active subscription. That was true when we only sold one product. We now sell three... So it's one active subscription per account per product.

ambiguities.description: Paused is described as 'a separate boolean' that 'behaves like a status' and 'overlaps confusingly' with the active status such that querying for active subscriptions also returns paused ones. It is unclear whether Paused is a genuinely orthogonal attribute or should be treated as an unofficial fifth status; the facilitator explicitly declines to model a fifth status but the overlap/bug behavior is not fully specified (e.g., can a cancelled or trialing subscription also be paused?).

source_references.excerpt: There's also paused. ... Paused isn't a status, it's a flag. ... It behaves like a status but it isn't one, it's a separate boolean, which is exactly why it causes bugs. If you ask the system for active subscriptions you get paused ones too. ... I'm going to record the four statuses as the status, and note that paused exists separately and overlaps confusingly.

ambiguities.description: MRR is explicitly derived/calculated (plan price normalised to a month) rather than stored, per Sam's clarification. However Sam initially called it a stored field ('It's on the subscription in the reporting layer'), creating ambiguity about whether MRR should appear as a materialized attribute in some reporting layer view even though it's not a base fact.

source_references.excerpt: Every subscription has an MRR. ... It's on the subscription in the reporting layer. ... It's worked out. It's the plan price normalised to a month. ... I'm not going to model it as an attribute of the subscription, then, because it isn't a fact anybody asserts -- it's a calculation over facts we already have.

ambiguities.description: The commercial/business rule for mid-term cancellation of annual subscriptions is explicitly left undecided (whether it should be run-to-term, prorated refund, or credit). Only the current system behavior (end date set to paid-through date, no refund mechanism) is modeled; four manual credits issued outside the subscription system are noted as exceptions/goodwill, raising the question of whether an unmodeled 'manual credit' concept exists that should eventually be captured.

source_references.excerpt: Mid-term cancellation on annual plans... What happens? ... Nothing happens. They've paid for the year, they keep access until December, we don't refund. ... the four Tom's talking about were manual credits raised outside the subscription. ... Put my name on wanting that resolved.

ambiguities.description: Sam and Priya briefly disagree about whether the subscription carries a stored 'current price plan' field at all, versus the plan being purely derived from plan-change history. Priya clarifies a denormalised current-plan field exists (maintained by the change process since a 'reporting rebuild'), and Sam withdraws his correction, but the exact relationship/consistency mechanism between the denormalised field and the change history (e.g., how disagreements are detected or resolved beyond 'the current plan is the bug') is left informal.

source_references.excerpt: One correction. You said a subscription belongs to one price plan. It doesn't, really -- that's what the plan changes are for. ... No, Sam, it does have a current plan field. ... Correct. And if those two ever disagree, the change history wins and the current plan is the bug.
